title: Self-testing ideal quantum measurements
authors: Debashis Saha, Zhen-Peng Xu, Adán Cabello
abstract: A fundamental prediction of quantum mechanics is that observables can be measured through ideal measurements, that is, measurements that give the same outcome when repeated and do not disturb any observable that is jointly measurable. In terms of quantum instruments, such an ideal measurement is described by projective effects together with the associated Luders state-update rule. Here, we show that quantum mechanics allows for self-testing any ideal measurement. Using solely the output statistics of bipartite Bell tests in which a non-demolition measurement is sometimes added, it is possible to certify in a device-independent manner whether the added measurement is ideal.
summary: This paper develops a method to self-test whether a quantum measurement is ideal using only the statistical correlations measured in a Bell test setup. By leveraging the Choi–Jamiolkowski isomorphism and analyzing conditional probabilities, the authors certify the ideal nature of the measurement instrument in a device-independent manner, even for complex, high-rank outcomes.
main_problem: The paper addresses the fundamental question of whether the ideal nature of a quantum measurement can be certified (self-tested) using only the statistical outcomes observed in a bipartite Bell test, potentially augmented by a non-demolition measurement.
main_result: It demonstrates that ideal Lüders measurement instruments can be certified in a device-independent manner by analyzing the output statistics, extending the self-testing capability to measurements with higher-rank outcomes.
method: The authors utilize the Choi–Jamiolkowski isomorphism to compare the unknown physical measurement operation with the ideal reference operation, employing techniques from context-projector games and Bell inequalities.
model_or_system: The system involves ideal quantum measurements, modeled by projective effects and the Lüders state-update rule, applied in the context of bipartite Bell tests involving three parties (Alice, Bob, and Carol).
key_observables: Output statistics (conditional probabilities) of the measurements, violation of Bell inequalities, and the robustness $R_c(M_c, P_c)$ of the instrument element.
important_parameters: The rank of the outcome projectors ($	ext{rank}(\Pi_c)$), and the dimension of the Hilbert space ($d$).
main_assumptions: The method assumes the ability to relate the unknown operation to the ideal one via pre-processing ($V$) and post-processing ($U_c$) operations, and relies on specific self-testing results for lower-rank outcomes.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the extended Bell experiment involving three parties. Figure 2 schematically represents instrument self-testing using the Choi–Jamiolkowski isomorphism, detailing the roles of pre-processing and post-processing operations.
paper_structure: The paper builds from initial self-testing of the shared state using Bell tests, progresses to formulating the self-testing of the measurement instrument via the Choi representation, and finally extends the proof to cover outcomes with higher projector ranks ($d_c \ge 2$).
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, device-independent framework for verifying fundamental quantum mechanical assumptions (like the ideal nature of measurements) using only experimental statistics, which is crucial for quantum information security and verification.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Extended Bell experiment involving Alice, Bob, and Carol. Alice and Bob perform measurements with inputs x, y and outputs a, b, respectively. Carol randomly decides whether to place her black-box instrument, producing out- come c and an unknown post-measurement system, before Bob’s device. The experiment therefore produces correla- tions {p(a, b|x, y)} and {p(a, b, c|x, y)}, from which Carol’s instrument can be self-tested to be sharp in a fully device- independent manner.

FIG. 2. Schematic representation of instrument self-testing via the Choi–Jamio lkowski isomorphism. The pre-processing transformation V identifies the physical input of the unknown operation Mc, while Uc extracts the ideal subsystem from its post-measurement output. In the device-independent realiza- tion, V is fixed by the initial state self-test as V = U † B.
